feedback: If only length is recorded, prompt in the moment: 'and which way is it pointing now?' and add a compass-direction column to complete the data, rather than reteaching the concept.

If readings are plotted in the order taken or as a bar chart with no time axis, guide the axis choice: put time on the x-axis and length on the y-axis, plot in time order and join the points so the midday dip appears — scaffold the axis choice, don't reteach shadows.

If the learner says the shadow changes because the Sun itself travels across the sky, address the geocentric idea: fix a lamp and turn a globe to show the Sun's apparent motion is our own rotation, then re-read the graph. When relating direction to the Sun, infer the Sun's position from the shadow (opposite to it) rather than looking toward the Sun.

Probe deeper with: 'Why measure at those particular times rather than all at once?', 'Your graph dips in the middle of the day — what is the Sun doing then?', and 'If you did this again in December, would the graph look the same? What might change?'
activities.intendedInsight: The daily shadow pattern lives in the DATA a learner collects and graphs: a U-shaped length curve (longest morning and late afternoon, shortest around midday) and a direction that always points away from the Sun and sweeps around through the day — a visible consequence of the Sun's changing apparent height as the Earth rotates.
learnerActions: Work safely outdoors: observe and measure the shadow cast on the GROUND; never look directly at the Sun — its position is found from the shadow, which points away from it.
Stand a fixed gnomon (e.g. an upright stick) in a sunny spot and mark its base so it and the recording paper do not move all day.
At four or more set times across the school day, measure the shadow's LENGTH with a ruler AND its DIRECTION with a compass.
Record each reading in a table with columns for time, length and direction.
Plot a line graph with time on the x-axis and shadow length on the y-axis, placing points in time order and joining them, using a sensible scale.
Also plot or draw the shadow's direction across the day (e.g. a compass-style fan showing how the direction sweeps around).
Read the pattern off your graph: when is the shadow longest? shortest? Which way does it point relative to the Sun?
Explain why the shadow is shortest when the Sun is highest, and link the daily change to the Earth rotating so the Sun appears to move.
activities.title: Build a shadow logger: measure and graph a shadow across the day

feedback: If the sequence or traced curve is flat or random, point back to the collected data and the midday-highest-Sun link.
Confirm correct ordering by checking the shortest length sits around midday, when the Sun is highest (not necessarily exactly 12:00 on the clock).
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidates that the daily shadow pattern is predictable and time-ordered: lengths follow a U-shape and direction sweeps around opposite the Sun.
learnerActions: Trace or sketch the expected length-vs-time curve for a day, placing the lowest point around midday, when the Sun is highest (by the clock this may be closer to 1 pm during summer time).
Put a set of shadow images or lengths in time order from morning to evening.
Match a given time of day to the correct shadow length and direction.
activities.title: Check and sequence the shadow pattern
